commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Add compact saga connector encoding experiment
commits.body:
A whole-codebase saga spends 230 MB restating one comparison identity and
133 notes across 532,290 diff references, and `change-saga query overview`
on it takes 17 minutes 30 seconds and 1.93 GB resident. This experiment asks
whether a compact, semantically sharded text encoding plus a disposable
SQLite index fixes that without making the evidence unmergeable.

It does, and the measurements say not to adopt it.

The encoding writes one human-readable `*.connectors` shard per (ownership
target, source path), hoisting the comparison identity and the notes behind
content-addressed aliases and writing contiguous changed lines as dense
ranges. It reaches 1.46 MB, 158x smaller raw. Every atom keeps the same
owners, notes, overlaps and stale verdicts, checked per atom against the
unmodified coverage.Evaluate in both directions and at both granularities.
Shards live inside the existing `___diffs/` directory, which a v2 loader
reads for `*.json` only, so a dual-encoded saga still loads and reports
identical coverage under an unmodified reader; dropping the JSON requires a
manifest version a v2 reader rejects loudly rather than reporting a fully
documented change as undocumented.

The result that matters is the control. Re-emitting the same evidence as
ordinary v2 JSON with ranged references -- a feature SPEC.md already has --
reaches 2.33 MB and takes `query overview` to 12.6 s. That is 98.9% of the
size and all 83x of the latency, with no format change at all. The 17 minutes
were a quadratic in reviewapp.session.build, which scans every selector a
target owns for every atom it owns; ranges collapse 1.19e10 scan steps to
about 1e8. Against ranged v2 the connector encoding adds 1.6x raw bytes,
nothing in the Git object store (1.01 MB against 1002.57 KB after
`git gc --aggressive`), and nothing measurable in load or evaluate. On a
sparse saga it is a regression: 5x larger deflated and 1.6x slower.

What survives is merge behaviour. `change-saga cover` names records by
timestamp, so two reviewers who explain the same lines differently never
conflict -- both records survive and the lines acquire an overlap neither
authored. Real `git merge` scenarios show the shards conflict instead, in
under twelve readable lines. That defect probably has a smaller fix than a
new encoding.

Everything lives in a separate Go module so the reference implementation's
dependency-light guarantee is untouched: the root module never sees
modernc.org/sqlite, and `go build`, `go vet` and `go test` at the repository
root are unchanged. docs/findings.md records the measurements, the
tradeoffs, the open questions, and the recommendation to fix the authoring
granularity and the selector scan instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Record why whole-codebase sagas are 230 MB and 17 minutes
commits.body:
A saga documenting an entire codebase — 532,290 changed atoms across 2,666
files, fully mapped, no overlaps, no stale references — takes 17 minutes 30
seconds to answer `query overview` and occupies 230.36 MB. Neither number is
a property of the format. Both are caused by three specific defects here.

`cover --changed-lines` copies one URI per changed atom straight out of the
comparison and never coalesces them, while the manual `--lines` path builds
ranged URIs from the same input. Zero of that saga's 529,599 line references
are ranged, which is not a plausible authoring choice; it is the signature of
the derived path. Coalescing takes the same evidence, with byte-identical
coverage, from 230.36 MB to 2.33 MB.

`session.build` calls cleanDiagnosticPath — filepath.Clean plus ToSlash, so
it allocates — inside its innermost loop, although the argument only changes
with the enclosing assignment. On this saga that is about 1.19e10 calls.

That same inner loop linearly scans every selector a target owns, once per
atom it owns, so the work is sum(atoms^2): 1.19e10 steps, of which one target
contributes 1.4e9. Ranged evidence takes it to about 1e8 and `query overview`
from 1,049.7 s to 12.6 s with identical reported coverage, but that only helps
sagas authored after the first defect is fixed. Sagas already on disk keep
their per-line references, and for them this loop is the whole problem.

The document also records what the compact-connectors experiment ruled out,
and one defect ranges do not fix: timestamped `cover` record filenames mean
two reviewers who explain the same lines differently never conflict in Git —
both records survive and the lines acquire an overlap neither authored.

Diagnosis only. Nothing here is fixed, and the document marks which claims are
measured and which are inferred from them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Emit canonical dense ranges from cover --changed-lines
commits.body:
`--changed-lines` copied one single-line URI per changed atom straight out of
the comparison, while the manual `--lines` path built ranged URIs from the same
input. On a saga documenting a whole codebase that is 529,599 line references,
none of them ranged, and 230 MB of evidence restating one comparison identity
half a million times.

Derived line atoms now coalesce into dense ranges. Coalescing is restricted:
two line atoms merge only when their repository, base, head, path, and side are
identical and their line numbers have no gap between them. A dense range is not
a widened selector — every line it spans is an atom the flag had already
selected — so the emitted URIs address exactly the same atoms, with the same
owners, the same notes, and the same overlaps. Events never coalesce; an event
is not a line and has no range spelling. Each identity is emitted once, at the
position of its first atom, with its dense runs ascending, so output is
canonical rather than dependent on hunk order.

Nothing about the persisted schema changes. Ranged line URIs are already what
`--lines 1-40` writes and already what `coverage.Evaluate` matches; the derived
path simply stops declining to use them.

The one behavioural loss is the one the diagnosis names: a dense range keeps
matching when a single line inside it stops being a changed line, so stale
detection for derived coverage is range-grained. In practice head identity is a
digest of the whole product patch, so any edit that changes the diff already
orphans every reference in the comparison, ranged or not.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Resolve selector ownership by identity instead of scanning
commits.body:
Session build resolved every coverage assignment by walking the owning
target's selector slice, normalizing each candidate's evidence path with
filepath.Clean along the way, and resolved every stale selector by
walking the whole orphan list. A saga whose selectors grow with its atoms
therefore cost O(atoms x selectors): linking 4096 selectors took 278ms,
and a saga eight times larger cost roughly sixty times as much.

Coverage already stamps each assignment with the identity it resolved --
target, evidence file, and the reference's position within that file --
so build now indexes selectors by that identity once and looks each
assignment up directly. Orphan reasons get the same treatment. Path
normalization is hoisted into a per-path memo, since coverage repeats one
raw evidence path across every atom the diff file owns.

Two evidence paths under one target can normalize to the same identity
(absolute paths are redacted to the empty string). The scan stopped at
the first such entry, so the index keeps the first one and the stale
reason lookup keys orphans by the unnormalized path the scan compared,
preserving both edge cases exactly.

Linking 4096 selectors now takes 4.6ms, and the new scale regression
fails if growth ever returns to quadratic.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Benchmark Open and query overview over per-line evidence
commits.body:
`change-saga query overview` on a whole-codebase saga takes 17 minutes, and
docs/large-saga-diagnosis.md attributes most of it to a quadratic in
`reviewapp.session.build`. Nothing in the repository reproduced it: the
generated fixture writes 1,024 four-line ranges over 144 fragments, so no target
owns more than eight selectors and the scan the diagnosis is about never runs at
length.

`testfixture.GenerateLargeSaga` can now write the other shape. `CoverageRangeWidth`
of 1 gives a reference per changed line, which is what `cover --changed-lines`
writes and what sagas already on disk contain, and `CoverageTargets` concentrates
those references on a few narrative targets, which is what a real saga looks
like. The default is untouched, so the byte budgets measured against it are too.

The benchmark holds one comparison fixed — 32 files, 4,096 atoms, the same tree
and review overlay — and varies only how its 4,096 references are owned. It
reports `scan-steps/op`: the exact iteration count of the selector loop over the
index it built, which is a property of the saga rather than of the host, so
`TestLargeSagaBenchmarkShapesRemainRealistic` asserts it where it could not
assert a duration. Nothing here asserts a wall-clock time or an allocation count.

Quartering the targets quadruples the scan — 4.1 steps per atom ranged, then
32.5, 128.5 and 512.5 — and construction follows it: 33.4 ms, 47.4 ms, 80.1 ms,
251.0 ms, against a flat ~33 ms of linear work and flat allocations.

Two things the measurement adds to the diagnosis. `Overview` answers in 0.2 ms
and 5 allocations whatever the shape, because it reads an index already built —
the 17 minutes is construction, not query. And `cleanDiagnosticPath` does not
allocate as recorded; `filepath.Clean` returns an already-clean relative path
unchanged. It costs 81.7 ns of CPU a call, which is about 172 ms of the
concentrated shape's 218 ms of scan, so the fix stands and the reason is
corrected in place.

No production code changed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Render the saga as a shell and fetch it as it is reached
commits.body:
GET / rendered the whole narrative tree: every chapter, every section, and
every explanation, with each explanation's Markdown read from disk, rendered,
and inlined behind a chapter disclosure that starts closed. That work was
proportional to the size of the story and almost none of it was on screen.

The saga document is now a shell — saga identity, coverage totals, the
overview's explanations as descriptors, one summary per chapter, and the
navigation outline — and the rest arrives from endpoints bounded by one node:

  /api/section   one chapter's structure, when that chapter is opened
  /api/fragment  one explanation, when it comes into view or is pointed at
  /api/locate    one anchor, when a permalink names something not on the page

The page's root render and /api/section share one scope, so a chapter body is
built by exactly the code that built the shell around it. Navigation and the
review progress map read the saga's manifests rather than the rendered views,
so they still name and count every destination while its chapter is unfetched.

On the 4,096-line fixture the saga document goes from roughly 2.41 MB and
71,000 elements to 39,126 bytes and 1,048 elements, and now tracks the number
of chapters rather than the number of explanations. In the browser the whole
first-load document goes from 555,974 to 414,626 bytes.

Three rules keep the boundary honest, each with a test: a descriptor is still a
destination, so permalinks and review decisions work before content arrives;
content is filled into the article that described it rather than swapping the
element under the reviewer's pointer; and anything that needs content asks for
it first, so arming an annotation tool waits rather than silently disarming.
<body data-shell-ready> says when the first fill-in has finished.

Fetching more often also exposed a snapshot that could outlive its inputs:
committing review records changes attribution without changing a byte under the
saga root, so the freshness check now commits to the saga repository's history
as well as to its bytes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Measure whether large-saga first run needs SQLite
commits.body:
It does not, and the measurements say why. On this repository's own saga
(38,209 atoms, 183 files, 814 saga files) a first-run snapshot costs 562 ms:
223 ms of saga.Load, 302 ms of two git diff subprocesses and their parsing,
and 37 ms of coverage.Evaluate. Ninety-three percent of that is reading Git
and reading the saga, which any cache consumes as input and no index can
remove. The 6.6% that is derivation persists to a flat gob file that reads
back in 37.5 ms -- a 15x win over rebuilding, available with no dependency.

Persistence also does not bound memory: decoding rehydrates the same 65 MB
heap. Bounded memory is a partitioning decision, and the server already reads
per source path, so a directory of independently readable parts gives it
where a query engine would not.

Two constraints settle the rest. Release artifacts build with CGO_ENABLED=0
for three platforms, so mattn/go-sqlite3 is not a tradeoff but an
incompatibility; and modernc.org/sqlite's nine modules run against a go.mod
with one requirement and a governance commitment to staying dependency-light.

internal/snapshotcache implements the foundation the design calls for and
nothing more: generations addressed by the fingerprints the server already
computes, so invalidation is addressing rather than a step that can be
forgotten; staged population published by one rename, so a reader sees a
complete generation or none; absent/building/ready with single-flight, so a
burst mid-build can be answered with progress instead of a second rebuild;
and placement outside every saga, so the Git-native tree gains no untracked
derived bytes and merge behaviour is unchanged.

It is deliberately not wired into the server. No handler calls it and root
HTML rendering is untouched, so this commit cannot change what a reviewer
sees.

Twelve tests pin the rules under -race. One of them found a defect during
development: a damaged generation correctly missed on lookup but still held
its name, so the rebuild's rename failed and the key was wedged permanently.
publish now removes damage and retries once.

Recorded separately in the design note, because it is larger than the
question asked: a WORKTREE head disables the snapshot cache entirely, so the
ordinary authoring configuration pays a full rebuild on every request. No
index fixes that -- the input genuinely changes -- but a git status probe
measures 40 ms against the 562 ms it would save.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Budget first load against comparison scale
commits.body:
The existing first-load budgets are ceilings over one fixed fixture. The
whole-codebase failure in docs/large-saga-diagnosis.md is not a ceiling
breach — it is a slope: 532,290 atoms across 2,666 files, authored as
529,599 single-line references, produced a page no browser opens, and a
budget measured only at 4,096 atoms passes throughout.

Measure the same first load over four fully covered fixtures that each
move one axis, and budget what may and may not grow with them:

  base      32 files x  64 lines,  4,096 atoms, 1,024 ranges
  deeper    32 files x 256 lines, 16,384 atoms, 1,024 ranges
  wider    128 files x  64 lines, 16,384 atoms, 4,096 ranges
  per-line  32 files x  64 lines,  4,096 atoms, 4,096 ranges

deeper widens the coverage range in step with the changed lines, so the
document and the authored evidence hold still while only the code grows;
per-line explains the same code the way the diagnosed saga did.

The asserted invariants are that the coverage audit renders exactly one
row per authored evidence range at every scale and never one per atom,
that the inlined diff rows do not move when the comparison gains four
times the files, and that four times the code costs the page 1.09x
rather than 4x. Two marginal coefficients are budgeted directly because
they are what decided the diagnosed saga: an authored range costs 3,357 B
of page and 3,640 B of resident memory.

Allocated bytes and retained heap are asserted; both reproduce to within
0.1% across repeated runs, and retained heap per changed atom sits in the
same regime the real 1.49 GB peak was measured in. The absolute
allocation figure is skipped under -race, which roughly doubles it, while
the growth ratios hold either way. Wall time is reported by
BenchmarkFirstLoadScale and never asserted: repeated loads of one
unchanged fixture varied by 3.9x on an idle machine.

Every fixture is checked for complete coverage before it is measured, so
no budget here can be met by a saga that simply explains less, and
TestScalingChangedLinesWithRangeWidthHoldsEvidenceConstant pins the
generator property deeper depends on.

TestFirstLoadMaterializesBoundedDiffNodes records what the page cannot
show: first load builds 2n + d diff view nodes for n atoms and d display
lines, and renders about 1% of them. Production rendering is unchanged,
so the accounting is pinned exactly rather than fixed, and removing it is
now listed as the largest remaining first-load allocation.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
